'''David John Tritton''' (26 July 1935 – 24 April 1998) was an English physicist who specialised in [[fluid dynamics]].

Tritton was born in [[Slough]] on 26 July 1935.<ref name="tritton">{{cite web|url=https://tritton.org.uk/descendants-of-henry-of-wickhambreaux/david-tritton-physicist|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110313060457/http://www.tritton.org.uk/descendants-of-henry-of-wickhambreaux/david-tritton-physicist|archive-date=2011-03-13|url-status=dead|title=David Tritton &ndash; Physicist &#124; Tritton Family History|accessdate=2014-08-26|date=2011-03-06}}</ref>  He was educated at the [[University of Cambridge]] and obtained his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] with a dissertation on "Experiments on Flow past Cylinders and Free Convection", supervised by Alan A. Townsend.<ref name="nodak">{{cite web|url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=127547|title=The Mathematics Genealogy Project - D. Tritton|publisher=genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu|accessdate=2014-08-26}}</ref>  Subsequently, he worked at the [[University of Newcastle upon Tyne]] in the [[UK]].  He was a visiting professor at the [[University of Texas at Austin]] when he died on 24 April 1998.<ref>Obituary: "David John Tritton", Harry L. Swinney and Peter A. Davies, Physics Today April 1999. http://scitation.aip.org/content/aip/magazine/physicstoday/article/52/4/10.1063/1.882637</ref>

Tritton is well known for his textbook ''Physical Fluid Dynamics'', first published in 1977, with a second edition in 1988.<ref>''Physical Fluid Dynamics'', 2nd Edition, D. J. Tritton, Clarendon Press, 1988</ref>
